translation:
  text: '“Now, sir, explain the mountains to me. Why do their forms differ so much?”
    “Listen,” he said. “These twelve mountains are twelve tribes[a] inhabiting the
    whole world. The Son of God was proclaimed to them through the apostles.”


    2. “But explain to me, sir, why the mountains vary and each has a different form.”
    “Listen,” he said. “These twelve tribes inhabiting the whole world are twelve
    nations. They differ in outlook and mind. Just as you saw the mountains vary,
    so the nations differ in their minds and outlook. I will also explain each one’s
    conduct to you.”


    3. “First, sir,” I said, “explain this: though the mountains vary so much, why
    did their stones become bright with one color when placed in the building, just
    like the stones that came up from the depths?”


    4. “Because,” he said, “all the nations inhabiting the world beneath heaven heard
    and believed, and were called by one name, that of the Son of God.[b] On receiving
    the seal, they had one outlook and one mind. Their faith became one, and their
    love one. Along with the name, they wore the spirits of the virgins. That is why
    the tower’s structure became bright with one color, like the sun.”


    5. “But after they came together and became one body, some of them defiled themselves.
    They were cast out from the company of the righteous and became as they had been
    before—or rather, even worse.”'
  philosophy: optimal-equivalence
  footnotes:
  - marker: a
    reason: textual_variant
    text: The second “twelve” is bracketed in the older working edition; the reported
      Athos omits it with “tribes,” and Ethiopic omits it with “mountains.” Sinaiticus
      has twelve tribes in its corresponding sentence. The next paragraph calls these
      groups twelve nations inhabiting the world, without supplying a map or identifying
      individual nations. Amherst190 fragmentg also partly overlaps this paragraph,
      but its “twelve” is wholly bracketed in the1901 edition. It does not independently
      certify the complete number/tribes sentence; fragmentg’s verso only partly overlaps
      paragraphs3–4.
  - marker: b
    reason: textual_variant
    text: “Of the Son” and the repeated “one” before “love” are bracketed in the working
      edition. Sinaiticus has Son-of-God name and one-love wording, with extensive
      damage and corrections in this paragraph. Its wording differs in how the calling/name
      clause is constructed. The draft retains the printed construction and does not
      treat all supplied letters as visible.
